title: My Journey With Building My Own Site With React
excerpt: From knowing almost nothing about React to building this personal website from scratch — the bugs, the struggles, and what I actually learned.
content:
When I first decided to build this website, I had one major problem — I barely knew React. I had mostly worked with vanilla JavaScript, some jQuery, and a lot of plain CSS. React felt like an entirely different beast.

The first week was pure pain. I spent hours just trying to understand why my components were not re-rendering, why state was not updating, and why the hell my CSS was breaking every time I made a small change. The famous 'Cannot read properties of undefined' error became my worst enemy.

What made it worse was that I was not following any proper structure. I was writing everything inside one giant component. My About section had become a monster with 300+ lines of code. That's when I realised — I was doing everything wrong.

Slowly I started breaking things down. I created separate components for Header, About, Projects, and Blog. I learned the importance of lifting state up, how to properly manage props, and why everyone keeps screaming about 'separation of concerns'.

One of the biggest challenges was making this website responsive. What looked perfect on my laptop looked like a complete disaster on mobile. Fixing the grid layouts, making the experience cards look good on small screens, and ensuring the blog cards didn't break the layout took me countless hours.

The design decisions were equally painful. Should I go with a dark theme? Should I use Tailwind or stick with plain CSS? I tried both and eventually realised that for a personal website, clean design with good typography matters more than flashy animations.

The most satisfying moment was when I finally got the About section right — with the experience cards, proper spacing, and that clean blue accent. It was the first time the website actually started to feel like 'me'.

This project taught me much more than just React. It taught me how to debug properly, how to break down complex UIs into smaller components, the importance of planning before coding, and most importantly — how to keep pushing even when nothing seems to work.

If you're also learning React and feeling overwhelmed, just know that it's completely normal. The struggle is part of the process. Keep building. Keep breaking things. And most importantly, keep shipping.

This website is not perfect. There are still many things I want to improve. But it's mine. I built it from scratch with my own hands, one frustrating bug at a time.

And that feeling — there's nothing quite like it.

title: The Paradox of the Absolute: Why Creation Might Be Necessary
excerpt: If the Absolute or God is already complete and self-sufficient, why does the universe exist? A personal exploration of a deep tension in Advaita Vedanta and classical philosophy.
content:
For a long time, I have been thinking about one of the deepest questions in philosophy: Why did the Absolute or God create the universe?

In Advaita Vedanta, the standard answer is that Brahman is purna — complete and self-sufficient. Creation is just lila, spontaneous divine play, without any purpose or necessity. The Absolute didn't need to create anything. It just happened.

But the more I think about it, the more this explanation feels incomplete.

Here are the strongest points that trouble me:

1. Spontaneous Lila Creates a Contradiction

If the Absolute is truly omniscient and the source of everything, how can anything be truly "spontaneous" or without intent?

True spontaneity implies something happening outside of will or knowledge. But if the Absolute is all-knowing, nothing can fall outside its knowledge. Calling creation "spontaneous lila" seems like a convenient way to avoid the question rather than answering it.

2. Relational Attributes Require Manifestation

Many attributes we traditionally give to the Absolute — such as omniscience regarding time, causality, and change — are relational.

Time is not a static thing that can be known in pure abstraction. It is a process. Causality is a relationship between events. These things only make sense inside a manifested universe. How can the Absolute fully possess these attributes in a state of pure, non-dual oneness where no time or change exists?

3. The Distinction Between Potential and Actualization

There is a fundamental difference between possessing infinite potential and actualizing it.

The Absolute may know itself completely and possess infinite creative potential. But knowing you can run is not the same as running. An unexercised potential is, in a meaningful sense, not fully real. Creation may be the necessary medium through which the Absolute moves from potential to actuality.

The very existence of this vast, complex, and finely balanced universe suggests that creation is not optional play, but serves a real function for the Absolute.

This is not a final conclusion. It is an honest exploration. The classical explanations feel too clean, too convenient. They seem to avoid the deep tension between "the Absolute is complete" and "the universe exists."

I believe this paradox deserves to be examined more seriously, without rushing to say "it is inexplicable" or "it is just play."

What do you think? Is creation necessary for the Absolute to fully express its nature, or is the traditional view correct?

title: PHP2Shell Explained: Inside Two Critical PHP Vulnerabilities
excerpt: An exploration of two reported PHP vulnerabilities, examining out-of-memory handling, memory corruption, stale pointers, and the potential for remote code execution.
content:
## Introduction

Recently, two critical PHP vulnerabilities were reported under the name PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618, associated with remote code execution, and CVE-2026-109619, associated with stale-state or use-after-free behaviour. These reported vulnerabilities are significant because PHP powers a large number of websites and web applications.

A vulnerability in the underlying PHP engine can affect applications that otherwise follow good security practices. To understand the reported issues, let us imagine the PHP engine as a busy restaurant kitchen.

## Section 1: The Restaurant Analogy

Imagine that every incoming web request is a customer's order. The PHP engine is the kitchen, memory is the counter space, and internal functions are the chefs.

Normally, the kitchen receives an order, prepares it, and cleans up before moving to the next customer. PHP follows a similar process by allocating memory, processing request data, executing application logic, and releasing resources when a request finishes.

### CVE-2026-109618: The Unfinished Order

Imagine a chef preparing an order containing one hundred items. The chef records that all one hundred items belong to the order. However, before the final item is prepared, the kitchen runs out of counter space. The chef is interrupted and leaves the order unfinished.

Later, the cleanup crew reads the order sheet and assumes that all one hundred items are ready. It attempts to clean up the final item even though that item was never properly prepared.

This illustrates the reported risk behind CVE-2026-109618: an out-of-memory condition can interrupt an operation before its internal data structures have been fully initialized. If subsequent cleanup code trusts the incomplete state, it may access invalid memory, potentially leading to memory corruption and remote code execution under exploitable conditions.

The important point is that running out of memory is not, by itself, the vulnerability. The danger comes from how the program handles the failure.

### CVE-2026-109619: The Stale Sticky Note

Imagine that a chef leaves a sticky note saying that an ingredient is stored in container B. The container is discarded, but the note remains on the wall. The next chef trusts the note and accesses the location where the container used to be.

That location may now contain something entirely different.

This resembles a **use-after-free vulnerability**. A program releases memory but continues using a pointer that refers to the old allocation. If the memory is reused, the program may mistakenly interpret unrelated data as a valid object.

The reported CVE-2026-109619 concerns stale internal state and unsafe references. Depending on the affected code path, this type of flaw can lead to memory corruption, information disclosure, or potentially remote code execution.

Both analogies demonstrate a common problem: software must not trust internal state after an operation has been interrupted or the memory it references has been released.

## Section 2: The Vulnerable Code — Understanding PHP's Memory Allocator

PHP is implemented primarily in C. This provides control over memory management but requires careful handling of pointers, allocations, and data structures.

The following function illustrates the pre-fix error-handling pattern described in the supplied research. Verify the exact source and revision before presenting it as verbatim vulnerable code.

```c
static ZEND_COLD ZEND_NORETURN void zend_mm_safe_error(
    zend_mm_heap *heap,
    const char *format,
    size_t limit,
    size_t size
)
{
    heap->overflow = 1;
    zend_try {
        zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, format, limit, size);
    } zend_catch {
    } zend_end_try();
    heap->overflow = 0;
    zend_bailout();
    exit(1);
}
```

### What does this code do?

- `heap->overflow = 1` marks the allocator as being in an overflow or memory-exhaustion condition.
- `zend_try` establishes an internal error-handling boundary.
- `zend_error_noreturn(...)` raises a fatal PHP error.
- `zend_catch` and `zend_end_try()` delimit the error-handling mechanism.
- `zend_bailout()` transfers control away from the current execution path.

PHP's `zend_try` mechanism uses concepts associated with C's `setjmp()` and `longjmp()`. In simplified terms, `setjmp()` records an execution context, while `longjmp()` transfers execution back to that context.

This mechanism can be useful for handling fatal errors. However, if an operation is interrupted while modifying a data structure, the jump may prevent the operation from finishing normally. Later code may then encounter inconsistent state.

In restaurant terms, the chef leaves before finishing the order, but the cleanup crew still assumes everything is ready.

### What changed in the reported fix?

The supplied technical analysis describes a change that handles memory exhaustion more carefully, allowing operations to reach a safer point before error handling unwinds execution.

The following simplified pseudocode illustrates the general idea. It is not a verified verbatim extract of the PHP patch.

```c
if (heap->overflow) {
    zend_mm_delayed_error(
        "Allowed memory size exhausted ..."
    );
}

return heap->fallible ? FAILURE : SUCCESS;
```

The design principle is to prevent an allocation failure from leaving partially initialized structures behind. Cleanup should occur at a point where PHP can safely unwind its execution state. Where continuing execution is unsafe, terminating the process may be safer than running additional cleanup code against corrupted state.

## Section 3: Why the HashTable Bug Matters

PHP uses a data structure called a **HashTable** to store key-value pairs. HashTables are used throughout the engine, including for PHP arrays and other internal data.

A HashTable maintains metadata about its contents, including how many entries have been used and how many elements it contains. The engine relies on this metadata when accessing, iterating over, and destroying entries.

Consider this simplified conceptual example of unsafe insertion ordering:

```c
/* Conceptual example of unsafe insertion ordering */
table->nNumUsed++;
table->nNumOfElements++;

bucket = allocate(sizeof(Bucket));
bucket->key = key;
bucket->val = value;
table->arData = bucket;
```

This is illustrative pseudocode, not a verified verbatim copy of the vulnerable PHP source.

### Why does the order matter?

The first two statements update the table's counters. Only afterwards does the code allocate and initialize the new bucket.

If allocation fails between these operations, the counters may claim that an entry exists even though the corresponding bucket was never fully initialized. The table's metadata no longer accurately describes its contents.

The problem becomes particularly serious during cleanup. PHP must release resources associated with arrays, objects, and other internal values. If cleanup trusts inconsistent metadata and treats an invalid bucket as a legitimate entry, it may operate on invalid memory.

In certain memory-corruption scenarios, control-sensitive fields may be interpreted incorrectly. This is one reason memory corruption in native code can potentially lead to remote code execution.

The restaurant analogy is simple: the kitchen has counted a dish that was never completed, and the cleanup crew attempts to wash it as though it were real.

An inconsistent counter does not automatically guarantee code execution. Exploitation depends on the exact implementation, memory layout, cleanup operations, and whether an attacker can influence the relevant data.

## Section 4: How Memory Exhaustion Can Become an Attack Surface

An out-of-memory condition can simply cause a request to fail. For a security vulnerability to emerge, the failure must occur at a sensitive point in the program's execution.

The supplied PHP2Shell analysis discusses multipart HTTP request parsing as one way of placing pressure on PHP's memory allocator.

Multipart requests are commonly used for file uploads and HTML form submissions. Each part can contain headers, metadata, and content that PHP must parse and represent in memory.

Several factors influence the memory needed to process a multipart request:

- The number of multipart sections.
- The amount of header and metadata information in each section.
- The number and type of form fields and file inputs.
- The relationship between request size and PHP's configured resource limits.

The size of a request on the network does not always correspond directly to the amount of memory required to parse it. Headers and internal data structures can introduce additional allocation overhead.

If PHP exhausts its memory allowance while modifying a sensitive internal structure, the resulting error-handling path may become security-relevant.

### Why configuration limits are not a complete defence

PHP provides settings such as `memory_limit`, `post_max_size`, `max_file_uploads`, and `max_multipart_body_parts` to constrain resource consumption.

These settings address different aspects of request processing. A limit on the number of multipart sections, for example, does not necessarily limit every header or every internal allocation associated with those sections.

The absence of a usable `Content-Length` header can also affect how a server processes an incoming request, depending on HTTP framing and the server integration. It should not be assumed that every chunked request bypasses all applicable size checks.

Resource limits reduce the risk of excessive resource consumption, but they cannot repair unsafe memory-management logic inside the runtime itself.

### Interpreting the reported fatal error

The supplied research notes include an example of a memory-exhaustion error indicating that PHP could not allocate additional memory, with the source location reported as `Unknown` on line `0`.

Such a message may indicate that the failure occurred outside ordinary user-script execution or could not be associated with a normal source location. However, the message alone does not prove that a vulnerability was exploited or that code execution occurred.

For defenders, unexpected memory-exhaustion errors on publicly accessible PHP endpoints are worth investigating, particularly when accompanied by unusual multipart traffic or other suspicious activity.

## Section 5: The Broader Significance of PHP2Shell

The reported vulnerabilities demonstrate why reliable error handling and memory safety matter in widely deployed software.

An application can validate user input correctly and still be exposed to a defect in the runtime that processes that input. Updating a content management system does not necessarily update the PHP interpreter used to execute it.

If a vulnerability allows remote code execution, an attacker may be able to execute commands with the privileges of the affected PHP process. Depending on the environment, this could expose application data, configuration files, database credentials, or other resources accessible to that process.

The actual impact depends on the vulnerable code path, server configuration, and permissions granted to the PHP worker. Not every PHP-powered website will necessarily be exploitable in the same way.

Organisations should verify the relevant security advisories, identify affected installations, apply appropriate security updates, and investigate suspicious activity. A web application firewall and restrictive process permissions can provide additional layers of defence, but they are not substitutes for correcting the underlying runtime defect.

## References and Verification

Before publication, confirm the CVE identifiers, vulnerability descriptions, affected code paths, and patch details against official PHP security advisories and the relevant source-code changes. The code excerpts in this article explain the concepts and should not be presented as exact vulnerable or patched source unless verified against the relevant PHP revisions.

The central technical lesson is that a program must maintain consistent internal state even when memory allocation fails. Error handling should not leave data structures partially initialized, and a pointer must never be treated as valid after the memory it references has been released.
